claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the synchrony of nucleation events among the metal species.
Matching the reduction kinetics of all metal precursors causes them to nucleate nearly simultaneously.
Nearly simultaneous nucleation of the constituent metals favors formation of a homogeneous alloy.
Asynchronous reduction leads to phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
Adjusting the heating rate or adding a chemical agent can narrow the kinetic window of precursor reduction and promote simultaneous reduction.
A fast-heating regime followed by a short dwell time ensures rapid and nearly concurrent nucleation across all metal species.
Synchronizing nucleation prevents formation of segregated domains.
The modified synthesis will yield a more uniform elemental distribution than the baseline.
The modified synthesis will yield fewer segregated phases than the baseline.
The modified synthesis will produce a lower decomposition-onset temperature than the baseline.
Formation of a true alloy rather than separate metal phases causes the lower decomposition-onset temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies when reduction kinetics are the dominant factor controlling phase formation.
The proposed mechanism may fail when high-temperature diffusion-driven sintering overrides initial nucleation events.
The proposed mechanism may fail when additives or surfactants fundamentally alter nucleation dynamics.
